diagrams.caption: Figure 1.1 Unemployment and real wage growth in 15 high-income countries (2010–2019).
diagrams.attribution: OECD. 2021. OECD Statistics ; US Bureau of Labor Statistics. 2021. International Labor Comparisons .

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this scatterplot chart, the horizontal axis displays the unemployment rate as an average of the years 2010-2019 in percent. It ranges from 0% to 20%. The vertical axis displays the real wage growth rate as an average of the annual growth rate of the years 2010-2018 in percent, ranging from -1.0% to 2.5%. The points on the chart correspond to the unemployment rate and real wage growth rate of 15 high income countries. The chart is divided into four quadrants that show different combinations of average unemployment rate and annual growth of real wages. The figure shows that for five large economies in Western Europe, namely the UK, Germany, France, Italy, and Spain, performances are disparate. Spain has a high unemployment rate and low annual growth of real wages, while Germany has a low unemployment rate and relatively high annual growth of real wages. The UK has a low average unemployment rate and a low annual growth of real wages.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.10 Indices for nominal wages, consumer prices, and real wages in the UK and Italy (2010–2022), with 2010 as the base year.
diagrams.attribution: Office for National Statistics . 2023. Istat . 2023. World Bank . 2023.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This figure shows two line charts for the UK and Italy for their nominal wage index, Consumer Price Index (CPI), and Real Wage Index. The horizontal axis shows the year, ranging from 2010-2022. The vertical axis shows the index, where 2010 = 100 is the base year. For both countries, the nominal wage index and CPI see an increasing trend from 2010, while in Italy, following the pandemic in 2020, the CPI sees a sharper increase while the nominal wage index plateaus. Italy’s real wage index remains around the its 2010 levels at 100 until 2020, when it sees a sharp decline to around 95. The UK’s real wage index is on a slight decline from 2010 to 2014, after which it is on an upward trend, and remains around its 2010 level of 100 in 2022.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.11 Labour market concepts.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this diagram, the horizontal axis shows Employment, N, and the vertical axis shows output per worker and real wage. There is a vertical line for the population of working age encompasses the entireity of the horizontal axis, and a vertical line for the labour force. The difference between the population of working age and the labour force is the inactive population. There is a vertical line at N to show the population employed. The difference between N and the labour force is the population who are unemployed.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.12 Output per worker is shared between firms and employees.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this diagram, the horizontal axis shows Employment, N, and the vertical axis shows output per worker (or worker productivity, labelled lambda) and the real wage. There is a vertical line at the end of the horizontal axis which represents the labour force. There are two horizontal lines from the vertical axis, one for the real wage (w), and one for the output per worker (lambda) which is above w. The difference between lambda and w is the profit per worker, and the difference between w and the origin is the real wage per worker.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.13 The wage-setting (WS) curve.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this diagram, the horizontal axis shows Employment, N, and the vertical axis shows output per worker (or worker productivity, labelled lambda) and the real wage (labelled w). There is a vertical line towards the end of the horizontal axis denoting the labour force. The WS curve is shown, it is upward sloping and depicts the relationship between employment, N and the real wage w. For a given real wage w_A, the point A on the WS curve corresponds with an employment of N_A. The difference between the origin and N_A is the number of workers who are employed, and the difference between N_A and the labour force curve is the number of workers who are unemployed.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.14 The price-setting (PS) curve.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this diagram, the horizontal axis shows Employment, N, and the vertical axis shows output per worker (or worker productivity, labelled lambda) and the real wage (labelled w). There is a vertical line at the end of the horizontal axis which represents the labour force. There are two horizontal lines from the vertical axis, one for the real wage (w), and one for the output per worker (lambda) which is above w. The difference between lambda and w is the profit per worker, and the difference between w and the origin is the real wage per worker. The Price-Setting (PS) curve is the horizontal line w.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.15 The WS–PS model of the economy’s supply side.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this diagram, the horizontal axis shows Employment, N, and the vertical axis shows output per worker (or worker productivity, labelled lambda) and the real wage (labelled w). There is a vertical line at the end of the horizontal axis which represents the labour force. The WS curve is shows, it is upward sloping and depicts the relationship between employment, N, and the real wage w. There are two horizontal lines from the vertical axis, one that intersects w_A which is the PS curve, and one that intersects lambda, which is above the PS curve. The difference between lambda and w is the real profit per worker, and the difference between w and the origin is the real wage per worker. The WS and PS curves intersect at point A, at the real wage w_A and the corresponding employment N_A. The difference between the origin and N_A is the number of workers who are employed, and the difference between N_A and the labour force is the number of workers who are unemployed.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.16 The mutual dependence between firm behaviour and the whole economy.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The flowchart shows the mutual dependence between firm behaviour and the whole economy. The aggregate real wage. (w) and unemployment rate (u) influence how individual firms act. Suppose there are 3 firms, they individually set firms nominal wages (W) and prices (P), which then affect the labour and product markets. The labour and product markets in turn affect the aggregate real wage (w) and unemployment rate (u) and the cycle continues.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.17 Labour market matching: flows, workers, and jobs.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: There are V vacant jobs and U unemployed workers. After recruitment, there are N employed workers and N filled jobs. Workers can move between jobs so that there are still N employed workers and N filled jobs. Workers can also leave the labour market, or jobs can be destroyed. When quits and layoffs happen, there are vacant jobs and unemployed workers. There can also be vacant jobs because new jobs are created, and unemployed workers because new workers enter the labour market.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.18 The reservation wage facing the firm.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this diagram, the horizontal axis shows employment in the firm, N, and the vertical axis shows the real wage w. There is an upward sloping line representing the reservation wage, i.e., the real wage required to employ N workers. It intersects the vertical axis at w^0_r. At point A, the real wage offered by the firm is w^1_r and the corresponding total employment for the firm is N_low. At point C, when the firm offers a higher real wage w^2_r the corresponding total employment for the firm is N_high.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.19 The firm’s reservation wage and no-shirking wage.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this diagram, the horizontal axis displays employment in the firm, N, and the vertical axis shows the real wage w. There are two upward sloping lines, one for the no-shirking wage and one for the reservation wage. The no-shirking wage curve is above the reservation wage curve. When firms set the no-shirking wage w_2, this corresponds with a reservation wage of w^1_r (which is lower than w_2) and total firm employment N_1.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.2 A model of the economy.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The diagram displays a model of the economy, and how firms, the government, and households interact with each other and the environment. Firms undertake the production and distribution of goods and services. Households consume the goods and services produced by firms and provide labour to firms. Households also provide labour, votes, and taxes to the government, which the government then uses to improve public services, write and uphold laws that determine how all the actors in an economy regulate their actions, and provide transfers to households. Firms also provide the government with goods and services and pay corporate taxes, and in turn benefit from public services given by the government.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.20 Deriving the wage-setting curve for the aggregate economy, the WS curve.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This figure shows two diagrams. In the first diagram, the horizontal axis shows employment in the firm, N^f, and the vertical axis shows the real wage, w. There are three upward sloping no-shirking real wage curves in the first diagram, the first shows the no-shirking real wage at high unemployment (at the bottom), the second shows the no-shirking real wage at medium unemployment (in the middle), and the third shows the no-shirking real wage at low unemployment (on top). Point A is on the high unemployment no-shirking real wage curve, where employment in the firm is low at N^f_1, and real wage is low at w_1. Point B is on the medium unemployment no-shirking real wage curve, where employment in the firm is moderate at N^f_2, and real wage is w_2. Point C is on the low unemployment no-shirking real wage curve, where employment in the firm is high at N^f_3, and real wage is high at w_3. In the second diagram, the horizontal axis shows aggregate employment, N, and the vertical axis shows whole economy real wage, w. There is an upward sloping WS curve, and a vertical line at the end of the horizontal axis denoting the labour force. Point A on the WS curve in the second diagram corresponds with point A in the first diagram, where there is high unemployment, so aggregate employment is low at N_1, and the real wage in the economy is w_1. Point B in the second diagram corresponds with point B in the first diagram, where there is medium unemployment, so aggregate employment is moderate at N_2 and real wage in the economy is w_2. Point C in the second diagram corresponds with point C in the first diagram, where there is low unemployment, so aggregate employment is high at N_3, and real wage in the economy is high at w_3.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.21 A wage-setting curve estimated for the US economy (1979–2019).
diagrams.attribution: Estimated by Stephen Machin (LSE, 2023) from Current US Population Survey microdata from the Outgoing Rotation Groups for 1979 to 2019. Data for men aged 26 to 64, with controls for age, education, race, state, and year.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this line chart, the horizontal axis represents the unemployment rate in the US in %, ranging from 16% to 0%, in decreasing order. The vertical axis represents the real annual earnings in 2019 $, ranging from $51,000 to $57,000. When unemployment rate is high around 16%, real annual earnings are low, and as the unemployment rate decreases, real annual earnings increase. This estimates an upward sloping WS curve.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.22 Determinants of the PS real wage.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this diagram, the horizontal axis shows employment, N, and the vertical axis shows output per worker (also called productivity, labelled lambda) and real wage labelled w. There is a vertical line at the end of the horizontal axis to denote the labour force. There are two horizontal lines intersecting the vertical axis, the price-setting curve intersects the vertical axis at w, and the output per worker line intersects the vertical axis at lambda and is above the price-setting curve. The difference between w and the origin on the vertical axis is the real wage, (W/P = (1-sigma)lambda), and the difference between lambda and w is the real profit per worker (lambda*sigma).

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.23 Equilibrium (structural), and involuntary and voluntary unemployment.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this diagram, the horizontal axis shows employment, N, and the vertical axis shows output per worker, productivity, lambda, and real wage, w. There is a horizontal line intersecting the vertical axis at lambda, and another horizontal line below this intersecting the vertical axis at w_A, which represents the price-setting curve. There is a vertical line at the end of the horizontal axis denoting the labour force. There are two upward sloping curves, the wage-setting curve and the reservation wage curve. The wage-setting curve is above the reservation wage curve. Point A is on the intersection of the wage-setting and price-setting curves at w_A and N_A. Point B is on the intersection of the reservation wage and the price-setting curves, at w_A and N_V. The difference between the labour force and N_A represents all the unemployed in the economy. The difference between the labour force and N_V represents those who are voluntarily unemployed. The difference between N_A and N_V represents those who are involuntarily unemployed.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.24 The WS–PS model, case 1: employment above equilibrium.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this diagram, the horizontal axis shows employment, N, and the vertical axis shows output per worker, productivity (lambda), and real wage (w). The price-setting curve is horizontal and intersects the vertical axis at w_A, and there is a horizontal line above the price-setting curve intersecting the vertical axis at lambda, denoting productivity. The wage-setting curve is upward sloping. There is an arrow from B to A denoting that that if the economy begins at point B on the wage-setting curve (N_B, w_B) where employment is above equilibrium, the economy will move towards the equilibrium point A (N_A, w_A) where both employment and real wage are lower.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.25 The WS–PS model, case 2: employment below equilibrium.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this diagram, the horizontal axis shows employment, N, and the vertical axis shows output per worker, productivity (lambda), and real wage (w). The price-setting curve is horizontal and intersects the vertical axis at w_A, and there is a horizontal line above the price-setting curve intersecting the vertical axis at lambda, denoting productivity. The wage-setting curve is upward sloping. There is an arrow from C to A denoting that if the economy begins at point C on the wage-setting curve (N_C, w_C) where employment and real wage are below equilibrium, the economy will move towards the equilibrium point A (N_A, w_A) where both employment and real wage are higher.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.3 The aggregate labour market.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The flowchart shows an overview of the aggregate labour market and how its components fit together. The population of an economy can be divided into population of working age, and the population not of working age (such as the young and the elderly). The population of working age can be further categorised into those who are in the labour force and those who are out of the labour force (i.e., are inactive). Those active in the labour force are categorised into the employed and unemployed. The flowchart summarises that the employed and unemployed make up the labour force. Adding those who are out of the labour force (inactive) produces the population of working age.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.4 Macroeconomic performance in the UK and US: employment, unemployment, and participation.
diagrams.attribution: Labour market statistics for the UK and US (2000–2023). International Labour Organization. 2023. ILOSTAT Database .

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The figure shows two line charts comparing the UK and US’s macroeconomic performances. The first line chart shows the UK and US’s employment and participation rates. The horizontal axis shows the year, ranging from 2000-2024. The vertical axis of the first line chart shows working age population in percent, ranging from 0% to 70%. The UK and US’s employment rates remain relatively constant from 2003 to 2006, with the US’s employment rate at a higher level than that of the UK’s. During the global financial crisis, both the US and the UK’s employment rates fall, although the former falls by a larger amount, converging around 2011. From 2012 to 2019, employment rates in both countries increase, the UK’s increasing at a faster pace and overtaking the US, and they both experience a decline in 2020 during COVID-19, with the US experiencing a more significant decline in employment rate. The UK’s participation rate increases at a slow, steady rate for most of this period. The US’s participation rate starts at a higher level than the UK’s in 2000 but begins a slow and steady decline in 2007 following the global financial crisis, falling below that of the UK’s in 2012. Both countries see a decline in 2020. The second line chart shows the US and the UK’s unemployment rate. The horizontal axis shows the year, ranging from 2000-2024. The vertical axis of the second line chart shows the unemployment rate in percent, ranging from 0% to 20%. The UK’s unemployment rate increases in 2007 following the global financial crisis and continues increasing until 2012. It steadily declines until 2020, where it increases slightly. The US’s unemployment rate increases at a faster rate 2007 during the global financial crisis but converges with the UK from 2012 to 2020. During COVID-19, the US’s unemployment rate sees a much larger spike than the UK’s, decreasing from 2021 onwards.

diagrams.caption: Figure 1.5 Labour market statistics for Australia, Germany, Norway, and Spain (averages over 2000–2019).
diagrams.attribution: International Labour Organization. 2023. ILOSTAT Database .

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This bar chart shows labour market statistics for Australia, Norway, Germany, and Spain. The horizontal axis shows the employment rate as a percent of the workforce, participation rate as a percent of the workforce, and the unemployment rate as a percent of the labour force. The vertical axis displays the labour market statistic in percent as an average of the years 2000-2019, ranging from 0%-80%. Norway has the highest employment rate, participation rate, and the lowest unemployment rate of the four countries, while Spain has the lowest employment and participation rates and the highest unemployment rate. Australia and Germany fall in the middle, with Australia having higher employment and participation rates and a lower unemployment rate.

diagrams.caption: Figure 10.10 The duration of democracy and inequality in disposable income (2015).
diagrams.attribution: Note: The correlation coefficient is −0.658. Michael Coppedge et al. 2025. ‘V-Dem [Country-Year/Country-Date] Dataset v15’ . Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) Project. World Inequality Database . 2025.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This scatter plot shows the relationship between years of uninterrupted democracy and inequality in disposable income in 2015. The horizontal axis displays years of democracy from 25 to 125. The vertical axis displays inequality in disposable income, measured by the Gini coefficient, ranging from 0.2 to 0.7. The chart shows a negative relationship: countries with longer democratic histories tend to have lower income inequality. Mexico, Brazil, and South Africa have fewer than 50 years of democracy and Gini coefficients above 0.6. The United States has about 50 years of democracy with a Gini coefficient near 0.47. European countries with longer democratic histories, such as Sweden, Denmark, and UK, have Gini coefficients between 0.2 and 0.3.

diagrams.caption: Figure 10.19 Stock market prices in Chile: the democratic election of a socialist president, 1970.
diagrams.attribution: Proprietary data from the Santiago stock market. Time zero is the first trading day on the Santiago stock market following the election. Daniele Girardi and Samuel Bowles. 2018. ‘Institution Shocks and Economic Outcomes: Allende’s Election, Pinochet’s Coup, and the Santiago Stock Market’ . Journal of Development Economics 134: pp. 16–27.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This line chart shows nominal share prices in Santiago (1969 average = 100) against trading days before and after the 1970 election of Salvador Allende. The horizontal axis covers trading days from −15 to +25, with day −1 marked by a vertical dashed line labelled “Day before Allende elected.” The vertical axis ranges from 70 to 160. Before the election, share prices were relatively stable, fluctuating around 145–150. Immediately after the election, prices fell sharply from about 150 to below 100 within a few days. The decline continued more gradually over the following weeks, stabilising between 75 and 85 after around 15 trading days.

diagrams.caption: Figure 10.2 The growth of government in the UK (1500–2021).
diagrams.attribution: Note: Pax Britannica refers to the century between the end of the Napoleonic Wars and the beginning of the First World War, in which (compared to earlier or subsequent periods) Europe and most of the world was relatively peaceful, with the UK the militarily dominant nation. The Glorious Revolution deposed King James II in 1688 and increased the independent power of parliament. UK Public Revenue; Patrick K. O’Brien and Philip A. Hunt. 1993. ‘The rise of a fiscal state in England, 1485–1815’. Historical Research 66 (160): pp.129–76.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This line chart shows the growth of government in the UK from 1500 to 2021. The horizontal axis displays years from 1500 to 2021. The vertical axis displays total tax revenue as a percentage of GDP, ranging from 0% to 40%. The chart has one data series, total tax revenue. Tax revenue remains close to zero until the 1600s, during the creation of the British Empire. It rises after the 1688 Glorious Revolution, increases during the Seven Years War from 1756 to 1763, and peaks near 20% during the Napoleonic wars from 1800 to 1815. During the Pax Britannica period, from 1815 to 1914, it fluctuates around 10%. It rises sharply during the First World War from 1914 to 1918, peaking at around 35%, before falling back. By 1928, at the time of universal suffrage, revenue is still below 20%. It rises again during the Second World War from 1939 to 1945, peaking above 35%. After the Labour party’s election under Clement Attlee in 1945, revenue stabilises at around 30% to 35%. From the 1979 election of Margaret Thatcher onwards, it remains in this range with minor fluctuations up to 2021.

Across all countries, the share of wealth held by the top 1% rises into the late 19th and early 20th centuries, then falls sharply around the First and Second World Wars. Since the 1980s, the share has stabilised at lower levels in Europe, while in the US it has risen again.

diagrams.caption: Figure 10.6 Democracies: origins, shortcomings, interruptions, and retreats.
diagrams.attribution: Note: Blank periods correspond to time periods when a country does not fulfil V-Dem’s coding period criteria. Four of these countries were electoral democracies with substantial voting restrictions prior to 1900: in two of them—Switzerland and France—almost all men (but not women) have had the right to vote since 1848. Either a light-green or dark-green bar indicates a date at which the country is designated by V-Dem as an electoral democracy. The dark-green bars represent CORE’s definition of democracy requiring that virtually all citizens have the right to vote (including, for example, women). assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This bar chart shows political regimes for 30 countries from 1900 to 2022. The horizontal axis displays years from 1900 to 2022, and the vertical axis lists countries. Each country’s timeline is divided into three possible categories: autocracy (electoral and closed), “democracy” with substantial voting restrictions, and electoral democracy. Most European countries, such as Switzerland, France, Belgium, and the UK, transitioned to electoral democracy during the first half of the 20th century, though many experienced periods of autocracy or restricted democracy in the interwar years. The USA and Canada are shown as electoral democracies throughout most of the period. Latin American countries such as Brazil, Chile, and Mexico, along with Asian countries such as South Korea, Taiwan, and India, transitioned to electoral democracy after mid-century, with interruptions by periods of autocracy in some cases. African countries like Nigeria and South Africa achieved electoral democracy later, mostly after 1990.

diagrams.attribution: The three categories of political system are based on V-Dem’s classification, so the electoral democracies include some in which substantial fractions of the population (for example, women) are excluded from voting. assets.alt: This area chart shows the share of countries in the world under three regime types—closed autocracy, electoral autocracy, and electoral democracy—from 1900 to 2020. The horizontal axis displays years from 1900 to 2020, and the vertical axis displays the share of countries as a percentage, ranging from 0% to 100%. Closed autocracy dominates the early 20th century, accounting for 80% of the countries in 1900. Its share continues to decline steadily, falling below 20% by 2000. Electoral autocracy begins with less than 20% of countries in 1900, rises after the Second World War, and reaches around 35% by 2020. Electoral democracy remains low before 1950 but rises sharply after the Second World War, reaching about half of all countries by 2000.

Spain’s unemployment rate begins at a higher level of around 2.5% in 1960 and rises rapidly at the onset of the first oil shock in 1973–74, plateauing at around 20% from 1984–1999. It then falls when the Eurozone is launched in 1999 to around 11% until the Global Financial Crisis in 2007 to 2009 when it rises rapidly to around 23%. Spain’s unemployment rate begins to fall from 2014, reaching around 15% in 2022.

diagrams.caption: Figure 2.26 The triangle of Danish flexicurity.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This flowchart shows the triangle of the Danish flexicurity bargain (political consensus). Employers are given the free hand in hiring and firing decisions, which is related to greater productivity and taxes. Therefore, there is income support if one is unemployed for a limited duration, perpetuating greater productivity and taxes. Given the limited duration of income support, there are incentives to remain in the labour force, such as labour market policies involving retraining and matching. This provides both employers and job-seekers with a larger pool of options, feeding into employer’s choices to hire.

The vertical axis displays the unemployment rate in %, ranging from 0% to 25%. Germany’s unemployment rate begins at around 1% in 1960 and starts to rise steadily at the onset of the first oil shock in 1973–74, plateauing at around 9% from 1994 to 2009, after which it falls steadily to around 4% in 2022. Spain’s unemployment rate begins at a higher level of around 3% in 1960 and rises rapidly at the onset of the first oil shock in 1973–74, plateauing at around 20% from 1984–1999. It then falls when the Eurozone is launched in 1999 to around 11% until the Global Financial Crisis in 2007 to 2010 when it rises rapidly to around 23%. Spain’s unemployment rate begins to fall from 2014, reaching around 15% in 2022. Denmark’s unemployment rate begins at around 3% in 1960, and rises moderately at the onset of the first and second oil shocks above Germany’s to around 7% in 1984. It fluctuates around this until 1994, and then falls steadily to around 4%, below Germany’s in 2009. It rises again moderately during the global financial crisis and the eurozone crisis to around 7%, and in 2022 it falls to 5%.

diagrams.caption: Figure 3.10a Growth rates of consumption, investment, and GDP in the UK and US, per cent per annum (1956–2022).
diagrams.attribution: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. 2023. FRED .

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This figure shows two line charts, one for the UK and one for the US depicting the growth rates of GDP, private consumption, and gross investment over time. The first panel shows the data for the UK. The horizontal axis displays the year, ranging from 1955 to 2025, and the vertical axis displays the growth rate of the three variables in %, ranging from -20 to 20. Gross investment is the most volatile, starting at a high growth rate of 15% in 1956, dipping to around 2% in 1960, continuing a volatile up-down pattern to steep declines in 2010 and 2020 to around -15% and -10% respectively, ending at around 10% in 2022. Private consumption and GDP show a similar pattern as that of gross investment, although with less volatile movements. Private consumption and GDP growth rates remain relatively stable from 1990 to 2009, and from 2010 to 2019. In 2020, both private consumption and GDP dip nearly as low as gross investment to around -10%, and recover to above 5% in 2022. The second panel shows the data for the US. The horizontal axis displays the year, ranging from 1955 to 2025, and the vertical axis displays the growth rate of the three variables in %, ranging from -20 to 20. Gross investment is the most volatile for the US as well, starting at around 0% in 1956, increasing to above 10% in 1960, continuing a volatile up-down pattern to a peak of 15% in 1985, and a low of below -10% in 2010. In 2022, the growth rate of gross investment is around 0%. As with the UK, the growth rates of private consumption and GDP in the US show a similar pattern as that of gross investment, but with less volatility. They remain relatively stable from 1990 to 2000, and from 2010 to 2019. In 2020, both private consumption and GDP dip below 0%, and recover in 2022 to around 5% before declining again.

diagrams.caption: Figure 3.10b Growth rates of consumption, investment, and GDP in Mexico and South Africa, per cent per annum (1961–2022).
diagrams.attribution: OECD. 2023. OECD Statistics ; The World Bank. 2023. World Development Indicators .

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This figure shows two line charts, one for Mexico and one for South Africa depicting the growth rates of GDP, private consumption, and gross investment over time. The first panel shows the data for Mexico. The horizontal axis displays the year, ranging from 1960 to 2025, and the vertical axis displays the growth rate of the three variables in %, ranging from -30 to 60. The growth rate of gross investment is the most volatile, starting at around 0% in 1961 and reaching a peak of above 50% in 1965, continuing a volatile up-down pattern, reaching its lowest point below -30% in 1995, ending in 2022 at around 10%. Private consumption starts out with large fluctuations between 1960 and 1965, beginning at around 5% in 1961, decreasing to almost -30% and then increasing to around 40% in 1965. Private consumption then stabilises moderately, fluctuating only between -10% and 10% for the remaining decades, ending at above 5% in 2022. GDP is the least volatile of the three variables in Mexico, its fluctuations are mostly between 10% and -10% throughout, mirroring the movements of gross investment and private consumption. The second panel shows the data for South Africa. The horizontal axis displays the year, ranging from 1960 to 2025, and the vertical axis displays the growth rate of the variables in % ranging from -20 to 20. Growth rate of gross investment is the most volatile of the three variables. It starts at around 0% in 1961 and hits a peak of 20% before declining to 0% again in 1965. In 1985, growth rate of gross investment in South Africa hits its lowest at almost -20%, continuing its up-down oscillation, hitting another low of almost -15% in 2020 before recovering to around 5% in 2022. Private consumption and GDP in South Africa have much less volatile growth rates than gross investment, but follow a similar pattern to it.

diagrams.caption: Figure 3.17 Consumption smoothing through our lifetime.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this figure, the horizontal axis displays time split into three periods namely “Start work”, “Promotion”, and “Retirement”. The vertical axis displays income and consumption. There are two paths shown over time, an income path and a consumption path. The path of income stays constant until the promotion and then increases to a higher level, staying constant at the higher level until retirement when it decreases and stabilises at a level lower than that after the promotion but higher than the level at which it started. The path of consumption starts low, increases at the “start work” period and then stays constant for the remaining periods at the higher level. The area between the consumption and income paths bounded by the time periods “start work” and “promotion” when consumption is above income is shaded and labelled “Borrowing”. The area between the consumption and income paths bounded by the time periods “promotion” and “retirement” when income is above consumption is shaded and labelled “Accumulating savings and repaying debts”. The area between the consumption and income paths in the time period after “retirement” when consumption is again above income is shaded and labelled “Running down savings”.

diagrams.caption: Figure 3.19 Consumption when households demonstrate present bias: an anticipated fall in income.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This figure shows two diagrams. Both diagrams display the path of income and the path of consumption over time. Diagram 1 shows the path of income and consumption over time in consumption-smoothing households without present bias. The horizontal axis in diagram 1 displays the time and is split into 2 periods, namely, “News about fall in income received” and “Actual income falls”. The vertical axis in diagram 1 displays income and consumption. The path of income starts at a high level and remains constant until actual income falls, falling to a lower level and staying constant at that lower level for the remaining time. The path of consumption starts at the same high level as income, but once news about fall in income is received, consumption falls to a lower level, staying constant at that lower level for the remaining periods. The area between the income path and the consumption path bounded by the time periods “News about fall in income received” and “Actual income falls” when income is above consumption is shaded and labelled as “Saving”. The area between the income path and the consumption path after “Actual income falls” when consumption is above income is labelled as “Running down savings or borrowing”. Diagram 2 shows the path of income and consumption over time in credit-constrained households with present bias. The paths of income and consumption in credit-constrained households with present bias are the same. They both start at the same high level and remain constant until actual income falls, falling to a lower level and staying at the lower level for the remaining periods.

diagrams.caption: Figure 3.2 The circular flow model: three ways to measure GDP.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This flowchart shows the relationship between firms and households, and how this is reflected in the measurement of GDP. Households spend money on goods and services produced by firms and supply labour to produce goods and services. This is the expenditure method to measure GDP. Income is received as wages by the labour force, and as profits by the firms from the production of goods and services. This is the value added by firms method to measure GDP, which is equivalent to the income method.

The vertical axis shows the growth rates in % of the variables, ranging from -50% to 60%. Growth of investment in new technologies remains relatively stable at around 10% from 1992 to 2000, and falls to -10% in 2002 during the recession. It rises back to around 10% in 2006 before falling again to around -10% in 2009 during the recession. After the recession, growth of investment in new technologies increases again 5%, remaining stable for the rest of the years. Growth of the Nasdaq index starts at around 20% in 1991, falling to around 5% in 1994 before rising again to around 25% from 1995 to 1998. In 1999 growth of the Nasdaq index peaks at around 50% before a dramatic fall to -50% in 2001 during the recession. It recovers to 20% in 2004, falling again to -15% in 2008 during the recession. In 2021 the growth of the Nasdaq index is around 40% before falling to around -15% in 2022. Growth of nominal GDP is relatively constant throughout the years at around 5%, falling to 0% only during the 2009 and 2020 recessions. In 2021 nominal GDP growth recovers to around 10%.

diagrams.caption: Figure 3.21 Low expected demand for the firm’s products creates a vicious circle.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This flow chart shows a vicious circle. Low expectations of future demand lead to low capacity utilization and low profits. This, in turn, generates no incentives to invest or hire, and consequently firms and workers spend little. This creates low expectations of future demand, and the circle repeats.

assets.alt: This line chart shows data for investment, aggregate demand, and business confidence in the Eurozone from 1996 to 2022. The horizontal axis shows the year, ranging from 1996 to 2022. There are two vertical axes. The vertical axis on the left shows the growth rate in % of 2 measures: Growth of demand (C + G + X – M) and Growth of investment (I), and ranges from -15% to 10%. The vertical axis on the right shows industrial confidence indicator as an annual average, ranging from -30 to 20. Industrial confidence follows the pattern of both investment and demand, where in 2009 when both the other indicators see a decline, the industrial confidence index falls from around 5 in 2008 to almost -30 in 2009. It rises again as investment and demand rise, and falls from around 5 in 2018 to below -10 in 2020, recovering to around 5 in 2022.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: : There are 2 diagrams. In diagram 1, the horizontal axis shows employment and the vertical axis shows real wage. Coordinates are (employment, real wage). The vertical line at the end of the horizontal axis is labeled labour force. The horizontal lines labeled PS curve intersects with the upward-sloping, convex curve labeled WS curve. This intersection is marked by point A, representing the supply-side equilibrium. The horizontal coordinate of point A represents employment at supply-side equilibrium, where there’s no bargaining gap. The horizontal distance from Point A to the vertical labour force line captures the corresponding unemployment level of 7%, labelled as structual unemployment. In diagram 2, the horizontal axis displays Output (income) Y in billions of € ranging from 0 to 100, and the vertical axis displays Aggregate Demand AD in billions of € ranging from 0 to 100. The coordinates are (Output, Aggregate Demand). There is a 45-degree upward-sloping straight line from the origin , labelled “Y = AD”. Starting at a point above 0 on the vertical axis, there is an upward-sloping straight line with a flatter slope than the 45-degree line denoting the initial aggregate demand function labelled AD(medium). Point A replicates its position from diagram 1, denoting the intersection of the 45-degree line and the AD line. Its horizontal coordinate is marked as Y_{SEE}, representing the output level at supply-side equilibrium. In diagram 2, two additional lines labelled AD(high) and AD(low) respectively are illustrated. These lines share the same shape as AD(medium) but are positioned above to represent boom and below to represent recession. AD(high) and AD(low) intersect the 45-degree line at point B (situated above point A) and C (situated below point A) repectively. B’s vertical coordinate denotes a higher aggregate demand value while C denotes a lower level. B’s horizontal coordinate is labelled as Y_{high}, indicating an output level exceeding the supply-side equilibrium. By contrast, C’s horizontal coordinate is labelled as Y_{low}, indicating an output level lower than the supply-side equilibrium. Both points are mirrored in diagram 1, with point B placed to the right of point A and point C to the left along the PS curve. Point B is below the WS curve while point C is above. At B’s employment level, the real wage captured by WS curve is 102, exceeding the real wage of 100 captured by the PS curve, and the 2% disparity signifies the positive bargaining gap. By contrast, at C’s employment level, the real wage captured by WS curve is 99, lower than the real wage of 100 captured by the PS curve, and the −1% disparity signifies a negative bargaining gap.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The line chart illustrates the relationship among UK GDP growth and real oil prices from 1950 to 2022. The horizontal axis represents the years from 1950 to 2022. There are two vertical axes: the first vertical axis shows GDP growth in percentages and ranges from −10% to 15%, while the second vertical axis displays real oil prices in ratio scale with the price in the UK in 1950 set as 1 as the base year, and ranges from 0.1 to 100. Two lines are plotted on the chart: one labelled ‘GDP growth’ and the other labelled ‘real oil prices’. The ‘GDP growth’ line exhibits fluctuations with no clear upward or downward trends, starting from 4% in 1950 and ending at just under 5% in 2022. The ‘real oil prices’ line demonstrates an increasing trend, beginning at 1 in 1950 and reaching almost 100 in 2022. The chart highlights three oil shocks. Following the first oil shock in 1973, GDP growth sharply declined from 6% to −3%, indicating a recession, while real oil prices increased significantly. The lines intersected in 1974, with the ‘real oil price’ line positioned above the ‘GDP growth’ line thereafter. The second oil shock in 1979, also due to significantly increased oil prices, led to a similar recession in the UK from 1979 to 1980, with GDP growth rate decreasing from 4% to −3%. The enduring third oil shock from 2002 to 2008 also resulted in a recession, with GDP decreasing from around 2% to −4%.

diagrams.caption: Figure 4.5 Supply-side equilibrium: claims on output per worker by workers and owners are compatible.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: In this diagram, the horizontal axis shows employment, and the vertical axis shows two measures: output per worker and real wages. A single vertical line represents the labour force, positioned at the far right of the diagram. Two horizontal lines are depicted: one indicating output per worker and the other representing the price-setting curve (PS), with output per worker positioned above the PS line. The upward-sloping, convex curve depicts the wage-setting curve (WS), intersecting with both horizontal lines. The intersection of the WS and PS curves is labeled as point A, representing the supply-side equilibrium. The horizontal distance between point A and the labor force line denotes the number of unemployed at the supply-side equilibrium. The vertical coordinate of A represents the real wage, expressed mathematically as W⁄P=(1-sigma)×lambda. The vertical distance between point A and the output per worker line signifies real profit per worker, expressed as sigma×lambda. The sum of these two vertical distances equals lambda, which denotes the output per worker.

diagrams.caption: Figure 4.6 Causal chain from lower unemployment to higher inflation.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The flowchart illustrates the causal chain from lower unemployment to inflation. When the unemployment level falls below equilibrium, the real wage captured by the wage-setting curve exceeds that captured by the price-setting curve, resulting in wage increases. This wage inflation subsequently raises firms’ costs, leading to price increases, known as price inflation.

diagrams.caption: Figure 4.7 Adding output to the causal chain from higher aggregate demand to lower unemployment and higher inflation.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The flowchart illustrates the causal chain from a rise in output to inflation. This increase in output is initiated by a rise in aggregate demand, which consequently causes the unemployment level to fall below equilibrium. As a result, the real wage captured by the wage-setting curve exceeds that captured by the price-setting curve, leading to wage increases. This wage inflation subsequently elevates firms’ costs, thereby causing price increases, namely the price inflation.

diagrams.caption: Figure 5.18 Policy interest rate and monetary policy transmission mechanisms.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This flowchart delineates the transmission mechanism of the central bank’s policy interest rate through the economy, culminating in inflation. The process begins with the policy interest rate shaping market interest rates, asset prices, economic expectations and confidence, and the exchange rate. These initial adjustments then simultaneously affect domestic aggregate demand and net exports. The resulting shifts in these components alter the overall aggregate demand. This chain of economic reactions instigates inflationary pressure domestically. In conjunction, changes in the exchange rate adjust import prices. Collectively, these developments result in inflation.

diagrams.caption: Figure 5.19 The nominal policy rate and market interest rates in the United States.
diagrams.attribution: Federal funds effective rates. FRED Economic Data.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The line chart displays the trends of the nominal policy rate and market interest rates in the United States spanning from 1970 to 2025. The horizontal axis depicts the years from 1970 to 2025, and the vertical axis that ranges from 0% to 20% captures the interest rate in percentages. The graph plots three distinct lines: the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage average, the corporate borrowing rate, and the policy rate. Overall, all lines show a sharp increase starting in the early 1970s, peaking near 20% in the early 1980s, followed by a consistent decrease until the early 2020s when a slight uptick occurs. Throughout the timeline, the mortgage and corporate rates move closely together, reflecting parallel trends in rising and falling rates. In contrast, the policy rate is more erratic, demonstrating pronounced fluctuations and divergences from the other rates, particularly after its peak in the early 1980s. Notable gaps between the policy rate and the other rates emerge in the early 1990s, early 2000s, and from 2008 to the early 2020s. These increasing gaps between the policy rate and market rates suggest that market interest rates do not always align closely with changes in the policy rate.

The process begins with the policy interest rate shaping market interest rates, asset prices, economic expectations and confidence, and the exchange rate. These initial adjustments then simultaneously affect domestic aggregate demand, denoted as C+I, and net exports, denoted as X−M. The resulting shifts in these components alter the overall aggregate demand, denoted as AD. This chain of economic reactions instigates inflationary pressure domestically. In conjunction, changes in the exchange rate adjust import prices. Collectively, these developments result in inflation.

diagrams.caption: Figure 5.21 A depreciation of the home economy’s real exchange rate raises output and employment.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This flowchart outlines the causal chain from a depreciation of the home economy’s real exchange rate to an increase in output and employment. Initially, an increase in the nominal exchange rate, denoted by e, leads to a rise in the real exchange rate, indicated by c. A higher c results in real depreciation for the home economy, causing exports X to rise and imports M to fall. These changes collectively lead to an increase in aggregate demand AD. Eventually, the increase in AD boosts both output and employment.

diagrams.caption: Figure 5.22 The exchange rate effects of a cut in Australia’s interest rate.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This flowchart illustrates the consequences of a cut in Australia’s interest rate sequentially. Initially, a decline in investment, indicated by I, leads to a decrease in aggregate demand and subsequently a fall in forecast inflation. This reduction in forecast inflation prompts Australia’s central bank to cut the interest rate, causing a depreciation of the AUD. Then, exports become cheaper while imports become more expensive simultaneously, leading to an increase in net exports, denoted by X−M. This eventually results in an increase in aggregate demand AD. Additionally, there will be inflationary pressures due to cheaper exports and more expensive imports, which offset the initial fall caused by the demand shock.

F., 2014. ‘Introductory macro-econometrics: A new approach’; OECD; ‘Three centuries of Macroeconomics data’, Bank of England; Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. 2024. FRED . Note: According to the Phillips curve model, when the series for the unemployment rate minus the NAIRU is positive, inflation should be falling and vice versa.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The line chart illustrates the relationship between inflation and unemployment in the UK from 1953 to 2023. The horizontal axis displays the years from 1953 to 2023, while the vertical axis, with values from −4% to 24%, indicates two values: the CPI inflation rate and the unemployment rate gap relative to the NAIRU. The chart depicts two lines: one tracks the CPI inflation rate,  the other line illustrates the unemployment rate gap, measured by the difference between actual unemployment rate and NAIRU. During the 1953–1967 fixed exchange rate era, the unemployment gap stayed close to the neutral rate, with slight peaks around 1960 and 1963, and inflation peaked at 5% in 1955, then fell and levelled at around 3%. In the 1967–1980 period, the flexible exchange rate period, the unemployment gap trended downwards from neutral to about −2%, while inflation saw a steep rise to 22% in 1975, then fell to 8% in 1978, and climbed back to over 15% by 1980. The 1980–1984 recession period shows the unemployment gap increasing from −1% to about 3%, and inflation descending from over 15% to just above 4%. From 1997–2020, a period marked by the Bank of England’s independence and inflation targeting, the unemployment gap was mostly around −1%, with a peak at 2% during 2008–2014, while the CPI inflation rate generally stayed close to the 2% target with a drop to around 0% in 2014. Lastly, between 2021–2023, the chart shows the unemployment rate gap dropping to −1% in 2022 before recovering to 0%, alongside a rise in the CPI inflation rate from about 2% to nearly 10% in 2022, then slightly dropping to around 7% in 2023.

The real exchange rate, after decreasing, fluctuates around 0.75, then rebounds above 1 post-2014. Three key annotations highlight critical phases within the time period from 1967 to 1977. Firstly, in 1967, the GBP depreciated within the fixed exchange rate regime, where the nominal exchange rate with a value greater than 1 indicates that a dollar cost more in pounds and vice versa. Secondly, after 1971, the UK had a floating exchange rate regime and the nominal exchange rate depreciated rapidly until 1977. Lastly, despite the nominal terms surpassing 1, the UK inflation was also significantly higher than US inflation, so in real terms the GDP appreciated, worsening competitiveness.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: This line graph depicts the rate of return on currency in the United States from 1900 to 2020. The vertical axis quantifies the returns on dollar bills, ranging from −20% to 20%, where the real return is defined as the negative of the inflation rate. The horizontal axis displays the years from 1900 to 2020. The line begins slightly above 0 in 1900, descending to its lowest of approximately −18% in the late 1910s and reaching peaks exceeding 10% in the early 1920s and 1930s, respectively. The graph shows considerable volatility in the returns throughout this period; however, this volatility diminishes significantly from 1940 onward, with the returns predominantly remaining negative. This suggests a persistent erosion of currency value due to inflation over the latter half of the century.

diagrams.caption: Figure 6.17b Real rates of return on three other assets, United States.

assets.alt: This line graph illustrates the real rates of return on three distinct assets—bank deposits, equities, and housing—in the United States from 1900 to 2020. The vertical axis represents the real rate of return, ranging from −40% to 50%, while the horizontal axis displays the years from 1900 to 2020. Each asset is represented by a separate line, with corresponding dotted lines indicating the average return for each asset over the period. The first solid line represents the real rate of return on bank deposits, which generally fluctuates 0%, indicating the average return over the period. Notable peaks occur in the early 1920s and 1930s, with returns exceeding 15%, while significant troughs occur in the late 1910s and 1940s, with returns dropping below −10%. After around 1950, the real rate of return stabilises somewhat, oscillating closer to 0%, with a generally positive trend in the latter half of the 20th century. Its corresponding dotted horizontal line represents the average return over the entire period, which hovers just above 0%. The second solid line represents the real return on a diversified portfolio of US equities, which exhibits significant volatility over the entire period. Notable peaks occur throughout the 20th century, with some returns exceeding 40%, particularly in the early 1920s and 1950s. However, there are also dramatic troughs, such as during the financial crisis of 2008, where returns dropped below −30%. Its corresponding dotted horizontal line indicates the average return over the period, which hovers around 9%. The third solid line represents the real return on housing, which exhibits moderate fluctuations over the period. Notable peaks occur in the early 20th century, with some returns exceeding 30%, particularly around the 1910s. However, there are also significant downturns, such as during the 1930s, where returns dropped below −30%. Its corresponding dotted horizontal line indicates the average return over the period, which hovers around 5%.

assets.alt: Advantages Disadvantages Debt allows people like Julia to consume before they have income (or, more generally, before they have enough income), or when their income is temporarily low . Debt also allows borrowers like Julia (or companies) to invest in productive assets, including housing, thereby raising future output. For Marco, debt has the advantage of providing a low-risk, or possibly zero-risk, future payment when he won’t have income. Both currency and bank money are forms of debt that provide crucial services as a means of exchange . Base money (currency and reserves) are both just government debt. They provide crucial services as a means of exchange and a unit of account . Currency also provides the unit of account : the way we measure prices. The central bank’s use of monetary policy to stabilize the inflation rate helps to stabilize the unit of account. Firms can use leverage to exploit the superior (but risky) return on productive assets, compared to the cost of borrowing. This in turn incentivizes them to find the most productive forms of capital.

assets.alt: Advantages Disadvantage Debt allows people like Julia to consume before they have income (or, more generally, before they have enough income), or when their income is temporarily low . Commitments to pay debt are fixed, so if Julia’s income turns out lower than expected, her consumption must fall, unless she defaults . Debt also allows borrowers like Julia (or companies) to invest in productive assets, including housing, thereby raising future output. As with borrowing for consumption, commitments to pay debt are fixed, while returns are risky, so debt makes the investment more risky (this issue is related to leverage ). For Marco, debt has the advantage of providing a low-risk, or possibly zero-risk, future payment when he won’t have income. But he almost always faces at least some risk of default . Both currency and bank money are forms of debt that provide crucial services as a means of exchange . Using bank money as means of exchange requires current account deposits that can be withdrawn on demand. This creates potential for bank runs; government-sponsored deposit protection schemes aim to prevent these. Base money (currency and reserves) are both just government debt. They provide crucial services as a means of exchange and a unit of account . But the value of currency is eroded by inflation, so it is a very poor store of value . Governments may also be tempted to use base money as a means of financing deficits, leading to high or hyperinflation. Currency also provides the unit of account : the way we measure prices. The central bank’s use of monetary policy to stabilize the inflation rate helps to stabilize the unit of account. Central banks may not be given enough autonomy to maintain stable inflation, especially if governments wish to use base money as a means of financing deficits. Firms can use leverage to exploit the superior (but risky) return on productive assets, compared to the cost of borrowing. This in turn incentivizes them to find the most productive forms of capital. But there are significant associated risks: leverage makes the underlying return riskier. This is a particular problem with banks (discussed further in Unit 8), which have a strong incentive to increase leverage.

assets.alt: Advantages Disadvantages They can reduce the risk of lending on their assets (compared to bilateral debt) by diversification (and to some extent, by inspecting the quality of the loans). But there is always some element of non-diversifiable risk, which must be borne either by shareholders or governments. They provide specialist lending to certain types of borrower (particularly households, particularly mortgages; also to small businesses). Increasingly commoditized via the internet. Their liabilities (bank deposits, or bank money) are a store of value . But they offer poor returns at long horizons due to inflation. Banks provide the means of exchange. In many economies this form of means of exchange has increasingly replaced the use of currency. Since bank deposits used for means of exchange can be withdrawn on demand, this introduces the risk of bank runs. Financial assets such as bonds and shares, traded in financial markets, allow households to invest indirectly in forms of productive capital that they would not be able to invest in directly. Returns on financial assets are often dominated by capital gains/losses , which can significantly increase risk, especially in the short term. Some economists argue that these price changes are driven by irrational factors, or bubbles. From Marco’s perspective, he’d rather lend to a bank than to Julia, because the bank can spread the risk by diversification. But there is always some element of non-diversifiable risk. Someone must bear this risk: either the shareholder of the bank or, if the bank fails, depositors may face losses. The government may also step in, so the taxpayer may end up bearing the risk.

assets.alt: Advantages Disadvantages Bond markets allow governments and corporations to borrow directly from investors. Financial intermediaries are an important source of leverage for corporations. Financial intermediaries are a source of leverage (indirectly) for households, since interest rates for long-term mortgages are to a great extent determined (via arbitrage) from bond markets. Pension funds allow households to save for retirement during their working life, and can reduce risk by holding highly diversified portfolios of financial assets. Returns on stock markets are risky, but are rewarded on average by higher returns, which are typically not affected by inflation rates. Financial assets such as bonds and shares, traded in financial markets, allow households to invest indirectly in forms of productive capital that they would not be able to invest in directly.

assets.label: Table 2
assets.alt: Advantages Disadvantages Bond markets allow governments and corporations to borrow directly from investors. Bond prices are very sensitive to changes in interest rates, resulting in risky returns over the short term. Financial intermediaries are an important source of leverage for corporations. Risk of default pushes up borrowing costs for risky borrowers, including governments. Financial intermediaries are a source of leverage (indirectly) for households, since interest rates for long-term mortgages are to a great extent determined (via arbitrage) from bond markets. Leverage has risks—the higher an entity’s leverage, the more its losses are magnified in bad times, just as the potential gains are magnified in good times. Pension funds allow households to save for retirement during their working life, and can reduce risk by holding highly diversified portfolios of financial assets. Most pension funds invest in risky assets. In ‘defined contribution’ pension funds, the household bears this risk. Other (‘defined benefit’) pension funds may make promises of guaranteed payments, while investing in risky assets, therefore with similar problems to banks. Returns on stock markets are risky, but are rewarded on average by higher returns, which are typically not affected by inflation rates. There is still significant non-diversifiable risk, from underlying productive assets, accentuated by leverage. Short-term fluctuations in stock prices can result in very significant reductions in wealth for those approaching retirement. Financial assets such as bonds and shares, traded in financial markets, allow households to invest indirectly in forms of productive capital that they would not be able to invest in directly. Returns on financial assets are often dominated by capital gains/losses , which can significantly increase risk, especially in the short term. Some economists argue that these price changes are driven by irrational factors, or bubbles.

diagrams.caption: Figure 7.19 An exchange rate regime is a monetary policy regime.

assets.label: Table
assets.alt: Exchange rate regime Monetary policy Flexible ( FlexIT ): level of nominal exchange rate set by global financial markets; stable inflation target The nominal interest rate is the key tool of monetary policy. With a stable target rate of inflation, a rise in nominal interest rates normally translates into a rise in real interest rates, and a real appreciation, which helps to stabilize the economy. But in the long run, real interest rates are determined in global financial markets. Flexible ( FlexNIT ): level of nominal exchange rate set by global financial markets; no inflation target The nominal interest rate is the key tool of monetary policy. But without a stable inflation target, rises in nominal interest rates often reflect upward shifts in inflation and expected depreciation rather than a change in real interest rates. But in the long run, real interest rates are determined in global financial markets. Fixed (credible): held constant against the dollar, or another currency No control. $$i = i^*$$ Inflation will be stable when it is equal to the other country’s inflation rate. Fixed (not completely credible): markets expect that the exchange rate may deviate from the level it is fixed at No control. Domestic policy rate depends on foreign policy rate and market expectations about the depreciation of the currency.

diagrams.caption: Figure 8.10 Positive and negative feedback in the housing market.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: There are two flowcharts. The first flowchart illustrates the negative feedback process where beliefs dampen price rises. The news that housing market is heating up causes price to rise, making some people to think price will continue to rise, thereby demand rises. But others believe price will fall again, eventually resulting in falling demand and stabilized price. The second flowchart illustrates the positive feedback process where beliefs amplify price rises. This scenario is also known as a bubble. The news that housing market is heating up causes price to rise, causing people to widely believe price will rise further, driving demand to rise. Such belief leads to price to rise, confirming expectations of further rises. As a result, demand goes up and price rises further. In turn, such price rises again confirms expectations of further price rises. Hence a cycle forms, which is often called as a bubble.

diagrams.caption: Figure 8.11 The price shock is dampened: negative feedback and stable equilibrium.

Their intersection is labeled as E, with a horizontal coordinate of Q^* and a vertical coordinate of P^. When the price is at P_a, a price higher than P^, the gap between D_a and supply that appears is denoted as excess supply, smaller than the gap of demand and supply. Another upward-sloping line labeled as PDC with a flatter slope intersects with the 45-degree line at point E mirrored from the first diagram.

diagrams.caption: Figure 8.22 Positive feedback processes that amplify a fall in house prices.
diagrams.attribution: The figure is adapted from the first two columns of Table 2 in Muellbauer and Aron (2022).

assets.label: Table
assets.alt: Channels and feedbacks Key mechanisms From falling house prices to aggregate output and employment Fewer houses are started and completed as profits fall in the construction industry. Consumer spending lowers as the value of collateral (in houses) falls. Amplification as households and the construction industry extrapolate falling prices into the future; lower incomes further reduce demand for housing. From falling house prices to the financial sector Mortgage arrears and foreclosures (repossessions) rise. Losses mount at banks, particularly on mortgage-backed securities (assets), undermining their net worth. Credit availability to the construction sector falls. Amplification occurs via contagion in the banking sector because of falling prices of bank assets, including via fire sales. From the financial sector to the real economy Amplification via feedback on real incomes Credit availability to the other sectors in the economy falls. Investment in new housing in other sectors falls. Consumption falls because of tighter credit and lower financial asset values, which reduce wealth below target and raise precautionary saving. From the real economy to the financial sector GDP falls and so do household incomes via the multiplier process ( Unit 3 ), causing a further drop in bank profits.

assets.label: Diagram

Therefore, the probability of banks failing increases, which in turn leads the government to choose to bail out banks. This eventually results in a cycle.

New plant growth in the Arctic, absorbing CO 2 , but may be too slow. Tropical rain forests and Northern boreal forests, stressed by drought; Amazon rainforests also deliberately burned to create farmland Reverse the carbon cycle and release CO 2 instead of absorbing it, for example, through the increased frequency of wildfires, triggered by lightning storms made more frequent by more volatile weather patterns caused by increased atmospheric humidity and other aspects of climate change. Stopping human-made forest burning and attempting to reforest. Risk is that local tipping points, for example, in the Amazon or African rainforests will be reached first. Human feedback Rising temperatures increase demand for air conditioning, increasing demand for fossil fuels and CO 2 release. Rapid transition to photovoltaic power generation would mitigate the impact.

diagrams.caption: Figure 8.27 Environmental dynamics, multiple equilibria, and the S-shaped EDC.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The diagram illustrates the environmental dynamics. The horizontal axis displays the sea ice in period t and the vertical axis shows the sea ice in period t+1. The coordinates are (sea ice in period t, sea ice in period t+1). A 45-degree upward-sloping straight line from the origin is labeled ‘summer sea ice unchanged from year to year.’ An upward-sloping, S-shaped line labeled EDC intersects this 45-degree line at three points: B, T, and G. Point B, located at a lower level, represents a stable equilibrium with little summer sea ice. Point T, located at a middle level, represents an unstable equilibrium, namely the tipping point. Point G, located at a higher level, represents a stable equilibrium with extensive summer sea ice.

diagrams.caption: Figure 8.28 Negative feedback processes stabilize a ‘good equilibrium’ on the left, and a ‘bad equilibrium’ on the right.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: There are two flowcharts. The first flowchart illustrates the negative feedback process where there is extensive summer sea ice. Initially, lower temperatures leads to extensive summer sea ice, which then results in solar radiation being reflected rather than absorbed. Less absorbed solar radiation in turn causes lower temperature, eventually resulting in a cycle. The second flowchart illustrates the positive feedback process where there is little summer sea ice. Initially, higher temperatures leads to no summer sea ice, which then results in solar radiation being absorbed rather than reflected. Less reflected solar radiation in turn causes higher temperature, eventually resulting in a cycle.

diagrams.caption: Figure 8.29 Stabilization of sea ice following a shock from G to E 0 .

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The diagram illustrates the environmental dynamics. The horizontal axis displays the sea ice in period t and the vertical axis shows the sea ice in period t+1. The coordinates are (sea ice in period t, sea ice in period t+1). A 45-degree upward-sloping straight line from the origin is labeled ‘summer sea ice unchanged from year to year.’ An upward-sloping, S-shaped line labeled EDC intersects this 45-degree line at three points: B, T, and G. Point B, located at a lower level, represents a stable equilibrium with little summer sea ice. Point T, located at a middle level, represents the tipping point. Point G, located at a higher level, represents a stable equilibrium with extensive summer sea ice. When the sea ice level in period t is at E_0, a point between the sea ice levels at T and G, it converges to point G. This convergence is indicated by arrows positioned in the space between the 45-degree line and EDC that point towards point G.

diagrams.caption: Figure 8.3 Positive feedbacks destabilize an unstable equilibrium and negative feedbacks stabilize a stable equilibrium.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The diagram illustrates a rounded hill surrounded by a deep valley. At the top of the hill is a ball that is not moving, but that may roll off the hill if a small force is applied to it. This depicts a tipping point or unstable equilibrium. If a force is applied, a positive feedback process takes the ball down the hill. When the ball is shown at rest at the bottom of the valley, a negative feedback process keeps it there at rest if any small force is applied to it. This depicts a stable equilibrium.

diagrams.caption: Figure 8.30 Climate change causes the EDC to shift down.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: There are two diagrams, illustrating the shifts in EDC due to climate change. In the first diagram, the horizontal axis displays the sea ice level in period t, and the vertical axis shows the sea ice level in period t+1. The coordinates are (sea ice in period t, sea ice in period t+1). A 45-degree upward-sloping straight line from the origin is labeled ‘Summer sea ice unchanged from year to year.’ Two upward-sloping, S-shaped lines labeled EDC and EDC′ respectively intersect this 45-degree line, with EDC′ positioned beneath EDC.  The line labeled EDC intersects at points B, T, and G while the line labeled EDC′ intersects at points B′, T′, and G′. Point B′, located beneath point B, represent the new stable equilibrium with very little summer sea ice. Point T′, positioned to the northeast of point T, represent the new tipping point. Point G′, positioned beneath point G, represent the new stable equilibrium with less-extensive summer sea ice. In the second diagram, the horizontal axis displays the sea ice level in period t, and the vertical axis shows the sea ice level in period t+1. The coordinates are (sea ice in period t, sea ice in period t+1). Three upward-sloping, S-shaped lines labeled EDC, EDC′, and EDC′′  are depicted, with EDC positioned at the top, EDC′ in the middle and EDC′′ at the bottom. EDC′′ intersects the 45-degree line at point B′′, representing the new stable equilibrium with extremely little summer sea ice. Notably, EDC′′ does not intersect the 45-degree at any other point, hence both the tipping point and the the extensive summer sea ice equilibrium disappear.

diagrams.caption: Figure 8.4 A poverty trap: lock-in due to risk aversion.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The flowchart illustrates how a poverty trap locks in due to risk aversion. The heightened risk aversion initially causes low yielding assets, which then results in lower returns on the assets chosen. Such lower returns eventually lead to limited wealth, which in turn leads to heightened risk aversion, resulting in a cycle.

diagrams.caption: Figure 8.5 Lock-in: the case of a poverty trap.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The diagram illustrates a rounded hill with a deep valley on either side. A ball is falling down one side of the hill towards a valley labelled as a bad outcome and another ball falling down the opposite side to a valley labelled as a good outcome. Gravity ensures that once a ball is in one valley, it cannot cross the hill to the other valley on the other side without a large force to push against the negative feedback of the valley.

diagrams.caption: Figure 8.6 The poverty trap dynamics curve (PTDC).

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: There is a diagram and below it a line chart. The diagram depicts a rounded hill with a deep valley on either side, with a ball at the top of the hill at rest. The line chart shows on its horizontal axis the wealth plus transfer of women in 2007 in USD PPP, and its vertical axis shows wealth in 2011 in USD PPP. Both axes range from 400 to 1200. A 45 degree upward sloping line shows a situation in which the wealth is the same in the two years. Initially, the poverty dynamics trap curve starts above the 45 degree line, then decreases below it, crossing the 45 degree line between 400 and 514 on the horizontal axis. The curve then increases to cross the 45 degree line once again at 514 on the horizontal axis, which is linked to the tipping point at the top of the hill in the diagram above. The curve on the line chart then continues to increase above the 45 degree line until around 800 on the horizontal axis, crossing the 45 degree line four more times in small deviations above 800 on the horizontal axis.

assets.alt: The line chart illustrates the distribution of income in the treatment group. diagrams.caption: Figure 8.8 The ratio of house prices to median income in the US (1945–2024).
diagrams.attribution: Home Price to Median Household Income Ratio (US) . Longtermtrends.

assets.label: Diagram
assets.alt: The line chart illustrates the ratio of house prices to median income in the US from 1945 to 2024. The horizontal axis displays the years from 1945 to 2025, and the vertical axis shows the ratio of house prices relative to median household income, ranging from 3 to 8. Initially, the ratio decreases from about 6.5 in the late 1940s to a low of 3.5 in the early 1970s. It shows a plateau with minor peaks of around 4.5 in 1980 and 1990. The ratio then increases dramatically from the late 1990s, rising from just above 4 to nearly 7 during the US housing-credit boom. Following the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers, the ratio falls significantly to below 5 during the great recession following global financial crisis. It then rises again during the COVID-19 pandemic, reaching around 7.5 by the end of 2024.

assets.alt: There are 2 charts. Both are line charts showing GDP per capita, measured in US dollars, for South Korea, China, and India from 1960 to 2020. Chart 1: The horizontal axis shows years from 1960 to 2020. The vertical axis shows GDP per capita in US dollars, ranging from 0 to 45,000. Three lines represent GDP per capita for South Korea, China, and India. South Korea’s GDP per capita increases steadily, forming a steep upward-sloping curve and reaching above 40,000 dollars by 2020. China’s line is flatter until the early 2000s, then rises sharply, forming a hockey stick shape and reaching around 20,000 dollars by 2020. India’s line rises gradually throughout the period and remains below both China and South Korea. Chart 2: The horizontal axis shows years from 1960 to 2020. The vertical axis shows GDP per capita on a ratio scale, ranging from 500 to 64,000 US dollars. The same three countries are shown. Two annotations on China’s line indicate ‘Beginning of reform period’ in the late 1970s and ‘WTO accession’ around 2001. All three countries show sustained growth on the ratio scale. China’s line shows accelerated growth after the marked events. South Korea has the highest GDP per capita throughout, while India remains the lowest but rises more visibly in this view.

Each country is represented by a separate line. Canada and the USA have the highest energy use throughout the period, both peaking in the early 2000s and then declining. Sweden follows a similar trend, though at a lower level. France and the UK show relatively stable use until around 2005, after which both decline. China’s energy use rises steadily from a low base in 1970 and overtakes the UK by around 2015. India shows the lowest levels across the period, with gradual increases over time.

India and China remain near the top throughout, with fossil fuel shares above 85% for most of the period. The USA and the UK show slight declines from around 90% to lower levels by 2022. Canada and France start lower and decline gradually. Sweden shows the most substantial reduction, starting near 45% in 1985 and falling to around 25% by 2022.

Each coloured band represents a different energy source: solar, batteries, nuclear, hydro, wind, natural gas, imports from outside California, and other (including geothermal, biomass, biogas, and coal).
